Global weather patterns are set to experience "far-reaching" consequences after the ongoing El Niño climate event surpassed all historical records several weeks before reaching its expected peak, the Met Office has warned.
Forecasting experts at the Met Office highlighted that the phenomenon, which has previously been termed a "super" or even "Godzilla" El Niño, broke earlier records well ahead of its culmination later in the season.
The naturally-occurring climate event develops across the Pacific Ocean when sea surface temperatures in the equatorial central and eastern regions become markedly warmer than average, disrupting standard atmospheric circulation patterns and substantially influencing global weather conditions as a result.





Professor Adam Scaife, head of long-range prediction at the Met Office, said: "We have been signalling for months that the developing El Niño will be an unprecedented event.
"The fact that it has already exceeded previous records, with several weeks to go before it peaks later this year, shows the enormity of this El Niño.

The unequal impact of the climate crisis on the world’s poorest people, including those in tropical areas, has been highlighted by new research that finds they will be among the last to feel the benefits if global greenhouse gas emissions are cut to net zero.
Temperatures have risen more significantly in tropical areas relative to their historic range than at higher latitudes, including in wealthier countries in Europe and North America.

Read more
A team of Australian climate scientists found this inequality would not be reversed if global emissions reached net zero – the implicit goal of the landmark 2015 Paris agreement – and could take “many decades to begin to reverse” if carbon dioxide was drawn from the atmosphere under a “net-negative emissions” plan.
The research coincided with the UN’s refugee agency releasing a report showing how the climate crisis was increasing the risk of people becoming stateless.
The climate inequality study, published in the journal Environmental Research Letters, was led by Dr Andrew King and colleagues at the University of Melbourne. They looked at three sets of computer modelling experiments of the likely temperature changes if global emissions reached net zero and overlaid the results with countries’ gross domestic product.


“If we follow a path that is close to net zero, then the inequality we see in present day warming persists indefinitely,” King said. “The wealthier countries that have caused more of the problem are not those that are the most exposed, even beyond net zero. The regions that have not caused the warming are those that experience the most warming.”
King said the fate of the planet’s poorest regions, which tend to be concentrated closer to the equator, would depend on how much greenhouse gas was emitted before the world reached net zero.
“Even when we get to net zero, we have still emitted an enormous amount of carbon into the atmosphere and its effects will continue for centuries. We can’t easily undo all that damage,” he said. “Getting to net zero sooner means we are less likely to have that long-term warming after net zero. We need to get to net zero sooner to limit that inequality.”
King said tropical ecosystems, such as some coral reefs, had mostly evolved to exist in a narrower temperature range than ecosystems at higher latitudes and would continue to be heavily affected for longer as the world cut emissions.
A separate report on the impact of climate change on the stateless, commissioned by the UN refugee agency and released with the Peter McMullin Centre on Statelessness, called on nations to support “the continuity of statehood” for countries facing extreme climate damage. In a small green meadow in the Gredos mountains, west of Madrid, a couple of dozen cows belonging to Juan Ángel Izquierdo and his family are grazing. The only noise is the gentle clang of the bells around the animals' necks.
This would be an idyllic scene were it not for the blackened pine and oak trees all around, the legacy of a devastating recent wildfire.
"It was immense, I've never seen anything like it," says Izquierdo, whose family have been farming here for 200 years.
The fire, in late July, merged with two others, burning a total of around 80,000 hectares (200,000 acres), making it the biggest blaze Spain has ever registered.
It consumed more than two-thirds of Izquierdo's land and killed 12 of his 85 cows. Another eight animals had to be put down because of their injuries. All the hay he had gathered to feed his cows in the winter was also burned.
"For us farmers, the summers are becoming more and more worrying, because they are getting hotter," he says. "It rains less, the wet season ends earlier and the autumn starts much later."
Wildfires
For farmers, such conditions are synonymous with fires.














"If you don't think about the wildfires too much, you feel okay," Izquierdo says. "But when a fire starts in a nearby village you start wondering – 'and what if we're next?'."
Wildfires are one of several symptoms of climate change which in recent years have had a substantial impact on Spain's economy, as well as contributing to shocking human tragedies.
World Weather Attribution, an international research organisation, found that the extreme conditions that drove record-breaking fires in Spain and Portugal in 2025 were 40 times more likely to happen due to the warming climate.
"The ultimate reason for the greater frequency and intensity of these kinds of fires has to be attributed to the increase in greenhouse gases caused mainly by the generalised use of fossil fuels," said Ernesto Rodríguez Camino, president of the Spanish Meteorology Association.
The Socialist Prime Minister, Pedro Sánchez, has described the fires in dramatic terms, placing Spain in the front line of an environmental crisis.
"The climate emergency kills," he said in July, during a visit to the southern province of Almería where a wildfire claimed 15 lives.

This year’s El Niño is already breaking records months before reaching peak intensity, with the world’s oceans recording 100 consecutive days of unprecedented heat.
El Niño, a natural warming of the eastern Pacific Ocean that shifts weather patterns globally, is already the third-most intense event on record, according to a new analysis. 
The temperature rise at the heart of El Niño in the Pacific reached 3.05C on 19 September, the highest daily reading in 150 years of modern measurements, according to Climate Reanalyzer, using data from the world’s top meteorological agencies. That exceeded the previous high of 3.02C in November 2015 and arrived two months earlier in the calendar year than that previous peak.





The figure is measured against the average sea surface temperature between 1991 and 2020. Another measure, ONI, which uses a rolling 30-year average and accounts for human-caused global warming, shows the event sits just a hundredth of a degree below the 2015 record. Both metrics draw on data from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
Averaged over August, the most recent full month for which data was available, the Niño 3.4 anomaly – a specific point in the Pacific used as a reference for the event as a whole – stood at 2.45C. That’s higher than every previous El Niño on record except the 2015-16 event, which peaked at 2.75C, and a reconstructed 1877-78 event which reached 2.7C based on sparse historical ship data.

El Niño events are classed as “weak” when the Niño 3.4 anomaly reaches 0.5C, “moderate” above 1C, “strong” above 1.5C, and “very strong” above 2.0C, climate scientist Zeke Hausfather explained. “For this year’s event, the Niño 3.4 anomaly has now reached 3.07C, which puts it in a statistical tie with the record set on 18 November 2015, set during a ‘very strong’ El Nino event.”


Averaging 14 seasonal forecast models, Mr Hausfather noted in Carbon Brief, the ongoing event was projected to peak at around 4.1C later this year, about 1.3C above the 2015-16 record.
Each of the 674 individual model runs in the latest analysis predicted a new record would be set. No forecasting system had previously been tested against an El Niño of this scale, he said, because none had occurred.



“The current El Niño event, which has been underway since June and is expected to last until next year, has been developing faster than any previous event on record,” Mr Hausfather wrote.

The “jaw-dropping” El Niño currently heating up the planet has burst through the highest temperature ever recorded for the phenomenon, several months ahead of its expected peak.
The latest data shows the temperature rise at the heart of El Niño in the Pacific ocean has now reached 3.05C. That is higher than the 3.02C set in late November 2015, the previous high set in the 150 years of modern records. This temperature is measured against the average of 1991-2020.

The preferred measure of most meteorologists uses a 30-year rolling average as a reference and so takes account of human-caused global heating. This metric, called ONI (Nino3.4), is on the brink of breaking the record, just one-hundredth of a degree below the 2015 record. Both metrics are underpinned by data from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).


View image in fullscreen
Damaged beachfront homes in Dana Point, California. Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty Images
The most recent forecasts predict a peak of 4.0C in November and December, according to the average of 14 different models assessed by climate scientist Zeke Hausfather. That is a level so far above previous events that Hausfather called it “mind-blowing”, while others have described it as “Godzilla-level”. Any temperature rise above 0.5C is deemed an El Niño; above 2C is called a super El Niño.


The current El Niño is likely to be the largest in at least 1,000 years and will pile extra heat into an atmosphere in which temperatures are already rising rapidly due to human-caused global heating. This double whammy means 2027 is set to “blow apart” previous records and become the hottest year ever recorded.
The climate crisis, caused by pollution from fossil fuels, is already supercharging extreme weather and killing people. The El Niño will ratchet up the impacts even further, and has already begun to affect regions across the planet as weather patterns are altered.


View image in fullscreen
The Panamanian-flagged LPG tanker G. SPIRIT on the Panama Canal. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images


“Very strong El Niño events like those in 1997/1998 and 2015/2016 were associated with hundreds of billions of dollars in damages globally - this event is leaving those past ones in the dust,” said Hausfather, whose is a contributor to Carbon Brief.
Prof Friederike Otto, at Imperial College London, said: “This event is a huge redistribution of energy in the climate system and is dangerous because it is unfolding on top of a much warmer, human-influenced climate system.
“So, in many places around the world we will see never-before-experienced heat extremes, with all their consequences on health, food security and water stress,” she said. “El Niño comes and goes, but as long as we continue to burn fossil fuels it occurs on an increasingly hotter baseline, making it much more difficult for communities to deal with the consequences.”

Vaccines for ash trees, skin treatments for newts and gene-edited swallowtail butterflies are among 14 tax-funded projects from the UK’s “invention agency” aiming to accelerate nature’s ability to adapt to the climate crisis.
The £54m accelerated adaptation programme from the UK’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency (Aria) – a public body that funds high-risk, high-reward tech projects – aims to investigate applications of biotechnology that can speed up wild species’ evolution and help them to adapt to new threats such as global warming and disease.

The 14 teams announced on Monday will receive a share of an initial £30m in grants over the next two years. They will develop tools to protect native British wildlife species, including the English oak tree and critical pollinators such as the buff-tailed bumblebee, said Yannick Wurm, the director of the accelerated adaptation programme at Aria.


View image in fullscreen
A buff-tailed bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) on Marlborough Downs in Wiltshire, England. Photograph: Nick Upton/Alamy
The world’s natural environments are changing so rapidly owing to the climate crisis and human pressures that many species can no longer adapt quickly enough, said Wurm, a professor of evolutionary genomics at Queen Mary University, London. “This cohort is a first exploration of how we can harness some of the powers of biotechnology to responsibly help wild animals and plants to overcome challenges they face,” he added.


The projects aim to work alongside conventional nature conservation measures, such as protected reserves, to give environmentalists a new set of “precision tools” that Wurm compares to mRNA vaccines for humans.
Aria is the brainchild of Dominic Cummings, the former chief adviser to Boris Johnson, who said it would fund “crazy” ideas that could “restore Britain’s place as a scientific superpower”.
The publicly funded body has attracted criticism for its research into controversial geoengineering techniques and grants that have given millions in UK taxpayer money to US tech companies and venture capital firms. Matt Clifford, Aria’s chair, was forced to stand down this month over what one senior MP called a “clear conflict of interest” after taking a job with Anthropic, the developer of the AI chatbot Claude.
One team announced on Monday, led by researchers at the University of Exeter, will use Crispr-Cas9 gene-editing on the swallowtail, a butterfly on Britain’s red list of endangered species, to increase its resistance to insecticides used widely on farms. On her first day as an expert author on the world’s most important climate reports, Prof Julia Steinberger knew nobody else, so she sat down at a stranger’s table for breakfast.
“Hi, I’m Julia. I’m from the University of Lausanne,” she said. The man across the table replied: “I’m Mustafa Babiker. I work with Saudi Aramco.”

Aramco, Saudi Arabia’s state oil company, is responsible for more of the carbon emissions driving the escalating climate crisis than any other company in history, and the kingdom has long been a major blocker of climate action.
Wasn’t that a conflict of interest, Steinberger asked. The UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), on which they both now sat, produces the reports that underpin UN climate negotiations and inform national climate policy around the world. No, Steinberger recalls Babiker saying: he had declared the relationship on the IPCC’s conflict of interest form. “That didn’t seem to me a very good answer, but he was friendly and we had a very nice breakfast.”

His appointment as a coordinating lead author for the IPCC’s coming Seventh Assessment Report sparked controversy in the climate science community last year. At least a dozen IPCC lead authors are employed by or linked to Saudi Aramco, Saudi institutions and other oil and gas interests, the investigation found. One IPCC vice-chair, part of the body’s leadership group, also represents the kingdom at global climate negotiations as a government employee.

In a world of wars and climate crisis, a new leader could save the UN. But would Trump allow it?

As the organisation meets this week, it remains the best hope for restoring order. But it relies on goodwill from the US president – and that is lacking





If all goes to plan, at some stage in the coming weeks 15 diplomats will emerge from a small sound-proofed room deep in the bowels of the United Nations headquarters in New York and announce the organisation’s next secretary-general.
The person they choose will face a combination of challenges unlike any that their predecessors have had to deal with. Two of the security council’s permanent members, the US and Russia, are engaged in wars of choice that have no end in sight. A UN commission of inquiry has accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza, but the UN has effectively been reduced to the role of bystander, pushed out by Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. The climate crisis is creating a cascade of new humanitarian disasters, while every day now seems to bring a new security threat caused by the unregulated rise of AI.



All of this is happening in a world in which the very principles of the UN – multilateralism, a rules-based order and international law – are under threat.
Secretary-general elections have rarely been this consequential and conversations about who should win will dominate the sidelines of the UN general assembly this week and next, as world leaders gather for the annual summit.
The UN, and the world it speaks for, desperately needs a new leader who is both charismatic and competent. Yet the five permanent members of the security council – the US, UK, France, Russia and China – hold a veto. Anyone who wants the job will need the approval of Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and, most importantly, Trump.
It is not easy to argue you are best placed to save the UN when the man you need to persuade would rather it fails.
Three informal straw polls have taken place so far and no frontrunner has emerged, indeed opposition to the two leading candidates rose in last Friday’s vote. Ten years ago, the election of António Guterres of Portugal was widely welcomed as a shot in the arm for the UN after a decade of the low-energy leadership of the South Korean Ban Ki-moon. In his previous role as the UN’s refugee chief he had been an outspoken activist and had pledged to continue speaking up for the world’s most vulnerable people. Then, a month later, Trump took office as the US president.

‘Do you have to be dead?’: US coalminers plead for benefits as black-lung disease cases surge


Trump says he digs coal – but pneumoconiosis cases are at a 50-year high, and sick miners are mired in benefit delays




For 38 years, Josh Armes worked as a coal miner in West Virginia and Virginia.
After retirement, Armes, 74, of Grundy, Virginia, was diagnosed with black lung disease, medically known as coal workers’ pneumoconiosis (CWP), caused by breathing in coal dust over long periods, which irreversibly damages the lungs.

Armes has required an oxygen tank to breathe for the pastfour years or so, along with regular doctor visits and an albuterol inhaler to help when he has trouble breathing. Even with the supplemental oxygen, he’s severely limited in what he can physically do.
In 2014, Armes received notice that the federal black lung benefits he had been receiving for more than three years were being appealed against by a coal operator. For the last 12 years, he and his family have been in an appeals process limbo, trying to regain their benefits while Armes’s condition progresses.
The federal black lung program was created in 1969 to provide coal miners disabled by black lung with monetary compensation and medical benefits. But the Armes family is just one of many who have struggled with appeals and long delays in obtaining federal black lung benefits.

Those delays come as the Trump administration moves to boost the coal industry and as cases of black lung are surging – reaching a nearly 50-year high, according to data published in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine last month.


According to a May report by the government accountability office (GAO), 7,709 miner beneficiaries were receiving black lung benefits in 2024. The report was requested in 2023 by Democratic senators Mark Warner, John Hickenlooper, Tim Kaine, and John Fetterman, who have also introduced legislation to improve the black-lung benefits system.
In the fiscal year 2025, about 22,500 beneficiaries, including dependents, survivors, and miners, were receiving black lung benefits.
Between 2013 to 2024, 40% of approved claims by the Department of Labor were disputed, generally by coal operators.
The May report said miners have expressed problems with obtaining black-lung benefits. It said miners have been forced to wait several years for their claims to be approved, and raised issues with coal operators filing appeals.
“I can’t figure out one thing. They sent me a paper that said I got first- and second-stage black lung. That ought to be enough, or do you have to be dead?” Armes said.

The accelerating climate crisis and this year’s record-breaking El Niño mean that, although the summer’s heatwaves are still fresh in the memory, households in the UK are already being told to prepare for a potentially destructive winter of storms and heavy rain – leaving millions of homes at risk of flooding.
Government action is needed to improve flood defences and build reliance on a national and regional level. But with the UK’s flood season just weeks away, the Guardian spoke to experts to find out what action communities and individuals can take to make their neighbourhoods and homes more resilient, from self-closing airbricks to deflated children’s footballs.

Community action
The first step is to check whether your home or neighbourhood is listed at risk of flooding on the government’s website. If it is, find out if the local council has a flood alert scheme and make sure you and your neighbours are signed up to that and the Environment Agency’s flood alerts system.
Join any local community flood group – or consider setting one up with neighbours – and approach the council to see what flood plans it has in place, and get involved in making them better. This could include lobbying for more permeable surfaces, rain gardens and tree planting.


Identify any vulnerable residents who might need extra support and draw up a street or neighbourhood flood plan to make sure everyone knows what to do in the event of a flood.
Tracey Garrett, the chief executive of the National Flood Forum, said flooding can be “incredibly frightening and disruptive” but insists that together, communities, households and councils can make difference to an area’s resilience.
“We are seeing increasingly intense rainfall and a growing risk from surface water flooding, and climate change means we cannot assume that the flooding patterns of the past will necessarily be the patterns of the future,” she said. “This makes preparation more important than ever.”
Gardens and outdoor spaces
According to Mary Long-Dhonau, who runs the Flood Mary campaign, protecting your home starts outside. She says now is an ideal time to check brickwork and mortar on outside walls for cracks or weaknesses. These should either be repaired or replaced and external walls can be treated with a breathable waterproof sealant.
“Having cracks or crumbling mortar can be like having 20 taps in your wall that will let the flood water straight in,” said Long-Dhonau, who provides a directory of builders who specialise in flood-related work.


Experts also suggest making sure gutters are clear and in good working order. Amid record-shattering heatwaves and popular demand for climate action, why are politicians often timid or in denial?




It was, according to the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, the “summer of truth”. Climate chaos ripped through Europe and the northern hemisphere, sending heat records tumbling, scorching crops in the fields, burning forests, emptying rivers and reservoirs, warping train tracks, melting roads and killing about 35,000 people in Europe alone.
The EU has estimated the damage at about €180bn, and the full bill is yet to arrive: harvests have been depleted, which will probably raise food price inflation, and expensive repairs to infrastructure have only just begun.

“All of this is a mere preview,” said von der Leyen in her state of the EU address on Wednesday. “These were the hottest summer months ever – but probably the coolest of the years to come. Science is clear. Europe is warming at double the global rate. Europe can, must and will stay the course on its climate targets.”


View image in fullscreen
Streets were flooded in Bangladesh this summer as extreme rainfall fell across Asia. Photograph: Monirul Alam/EPA

Extreme rainfall across Asia brought flash floods and typhoons, displacing hundreds of thousands of people and causing severe damage to crops.


So what has the political response been? Tepid at best from centrist and leftwing politicians, say campaigners, with few rays of hope to brighten the gloom; denial and dangerous, provocative incoherence from the right and far right.
“It was the hottest of summers – it was the meekest of responses,” said Magda Stoczkiewicz, the EU programme director for Greenpeace, of von der Leyen’s intervention. “The EU Commission continues its crusade to dismantle and defund environmental action. articles.jina_text:
This round-up of claims has been compiled by Full Fact, the UK’s independent fact checking charity which works to give people access to reliable information they can trust.

Solar panels don’t currently occupy ‘thousands of square miles’ of UK farmland




At Reform UK’s party conference earlier this month, the party’s chair Lee Anderson MP said in a Q&A session: “What we don’t want to see on farmers’ land is solar panels up and down the country. There’s literally thousands of square miles on farmland.”




This figure is not correct, and in fact it’s a substantial overstatement. Most land used for solar farms was previously agricultural land, but the total area of land estimated to be covered by them is much less than “thousands of square miles”.








In September 2024, ground-mounted solar panels covered “an estimated 21,200 hectares (52,000 acres)” or “around 0.1 per cent of the total land area of the UK”, according to the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ).




21,200 hectares is equivalent to approximately 81.9 square miles, or about 0.1% of the total UK land area of 24,438,000 hectares.




The DESNZ told Full Fact this remains its latest estimate.




Last year researchers at Lancaster University produced a slightly lower estimate of up to 17,364 hectares, or 67 square miles. They estimated that of this, around 10,118 hectares (39 square miles) may have previously been arable or horticulture land.




We contacted Mr Anderson for comment.




The amount of land used for solar is expected to increase in the coming years. The government’s UK Solar Roadmap sets out that “up to 0.4% of total UK land” could be required for solar by 2030, while other projections put potential land use as even higher. But even the largest future estimates we’ve seen are less than the “thousands of square miles” referred to by Mr Anderson.













London’s white population has not ‘plummeted to 34%’




Posts shared on social media have claimed that the white population in London has dropped to 34%. But that isn’t correct, according to the latest census data.




That data, which was recorded in 2021, shows that at the time 53.8%, not 34%, of people in London identified as white.









This includes 36.8% who identified as “White: English, Welsh, Scottish, Northern Irish or British”, plus a further 17% recorded as “White: Other”, which includes those who said they were white Irish, Gypsy or Irish Traveller, Roma or any other white background.




We’ve not found any more recent data reliably recording the ethnicity of London’s population, and no other credible evidence to support the 34% claim.

The fight within the Greens that led senators to cross the floor last week over koala protection in a national park may have finally put a spotlight on a bigger issue – one at the heart of much of Australia’s promise to act on the climate crisis. It’s this: the country and its polluting industries are too reliant on carbon offsets. The more reliance is placed on them, the more they look like a house of cards.
Offsets can be a mind-deadening subject, but they matter. In Australia, they are known as Australian Carbon Credit Units. Each credit is said to represent one tonne of greenhouse gas that isn’t in the atmosphere and otherwise would have been. They are mostly generated from government-sanctioned projects that are meant to regenerate forests or capture and burn methane released from landfill sites.

These type of projects have plenty to recommend them. With global heating moving into increasingly dangerous territory, the world needs to retain and regenerate all the forests it can, and create new ones. It also needs to sharply reduce how much methane and carbon dioxide is poured into the atmosphere.
But we need to be realistic about what these carbon credits can and can’t do.
Australian carbon credits are treated as a like-for-like alternative for emissions cuts by fossil fuel producers, factories and other big polluting sites. Under the climate policy applied to big industrial facilities responsible for about a third of national pollution – the safeguard mechanism – there is no requirement that businesses make direct emissions cuts. They can just buy an unlimited number of offsets and claim them as their own reductions.


This flexibility makes life easier for the owners of industrial sites that, under changes introduced by Labor three years ago, need to cut emissions intensity – the amount of pollution pumped out per unit of production – by between 1% and 4.9% a year. But it also creates problems.
Geologically stored carbon that is dug up and used as coal, gas or oil has been underground for millennia. When it is brought to the surface and set on fire it releases heat-trapping gas that otherwise couldn’t escape. That gas can persist in the atmosphere for thousands of years.

Clutching surfboards clad with slogans like “end sewage pollution” in gaffer tape, Giles Bristow – chief executive of Surfers Against Sewage – and a group of campaigners delivered their petition signed by 350,000 people to number 10 Downing Street earlier this month. Their message was simple: clean up Britain’s polluted water.
The charity has been campaigning on the issue for its entire 36-year existence. But this year, it's been thrust into the country's consciousness amid the extreme droughts and floods which have laid bare the extent of the issue – as well as through Channel 4's incredibly powerful and must-watch docu-drama, Dirty Business which the charity worked on. 
Dirty Business portrayed the story of Heather Preen, an eight-year-old girl who died in 1999 after contracting E. coli 0157 (the most dangerous strain) during a family holiday in Devon, following a sewage spill. Heather’s mother, Julie Maughan, has continued campaigning for cleaner water with the charity ever since and was also at Downing Street.

Recommended

The Climate 100 List: Engineer Joseph Nguthiru on turning the world’s most invasive plant into bioplastic
The petition is calling to “clean up” the government's proposed Clean Water Bill, and to end the broken privatised ownership of our water system that's been in place since 1989 that "pollutes for profit" and does "not prioritise the environment or our health," Bristow tells me when we meet at Surfers Against Sewage’s offices in St Agnes, Cornwall. 





Surfers Against Sewage is creating a groundswell for systemic change, with Bristow saying that for the majority of businesses "the only duty that exists is to return a reasonable profit to shareholders".





Andy Burnham cannot ignore this tidal wave of public opinion. This is just the tip of the iceberg of the people who care about this issue
The number of signatures show the public is increasingly unwilling to accept polluted rivers and seas as normal. "We're firmly putting this on [prime minister] Andy Burnham's agenda – he cannot ignore this tidal wave of public opinion. This is just the tip of the iceberg of the people who care about this issue,” Bristow says.


This summer has also made the issue even more difficult to ignore. During July and August, Surfers Against Sewage recorded more than 43,000 hours of sewage discharges into England’s waters, including more than 2,000 hours into designated bathing waters. Water companies are only permitted to discharge untreated sewage only following heavy rainfall and storms, when the systems are overloaded – yet it's been the hottest summer on record, with barely any rainfall.

More than 1,600 critically imperiled species protected under the US Endangered Species Act (ESA) face losing further federal protections following a new reinterpretation of the 1973 law by the Donald Trump administration.
A September 14 memo distributed to Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) field offices by FWS director Brian Nesvik calls for a reinterpretation of what it means to “take” an endangered species. Under the ESA, “take” is defined as “to harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture, or collect, or to attempt to engage in any such conduct”.

The memo, obtained and shared by the Center for Biological Diversity, reinterprets the law to mean that harming or killing an endangered animal would no longer be considered illegal unless the action was specifically intended to cause harm or death.



“A vessel that inadvertently strikes a whale has not taken it, because the vessel’s course was not set against the whale,” the memo said, adding: “Felling a tree is not a take of the bats roosting in it unless the tree is felled for the purpose of killing or capturing them.”
The reinterpretation effectively excludes economic activities such as logging, mining and industrial development from the ESA’s prohibition on “take” when those activities foreseeably kill or injure wildlife without intentionally targeting them.
The memo follows the Trump administration’s repeal in July of the ESA’s definition of prohibited “harm,” which was defined as “an act which actually kills or injures wildlife,” including acts that “may include significant habitat modification or degradation”.
Interior secretary Doug Burgum justified the repeal in July by saying: “For years, federal agencies abused the ESA to obstruct lawful land use and burden American families and businesses.”
Earlier this month, 20 states and Washington DC sued the Trump administration over its decision to redefine “harm,” including removing “modification or degradation” of habitat from conduct that can constitute a prohibited take.


In a statement on Thursday to the Guardian about the administration’s reinterpretation of “take,” the interior department, which oversees the FWS, said: “As outlined in the final rule, the department determined that the previous regulatory definition of ‘harm’ expanded the Endangered Species Act’s prohibition on ‘take’ beyond the text Congress enacted. Editorial





New research links last month’s disaster to fossil fuel pollution. Supporting disaster-hit countries must be at the centre of climate politics





Following a familiar pattern, coverage of the glacier collapse on the Nepal-Tibet border three weeks ago has subsided with the initial shock. But while the world’s attention has shifted, Nepal remains in the midst of an appalling tragedy. As well as at least 1,300 people who are known to have been killed, more than 5,000 are missing, some of them trapped in tunnels linked to the 13 hydropower plants that were damaged by the floods. On Wednesday four bodies were recovered from one of these tunnels, with searches ongoing. Families of the missing people are desperate for news.
Last week the country’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, said that it would ask the UN’s loss and damage fund for $20m (£15m) towards a total rebuilding cost of around $5bn (£3.75bn) – including the replacement of up to 20,000 homes. The first academic study linking the disaster to the climate crisis will now be added to that application. Scientists at Imperial College London, along with international collaborators on the World Weather Attribution project, found that a number of drivers of the glacier fall had been made worse by atmospheric heating. While not the sole cause, fossil fuel pollution was judged to have destabilised the geology of the mountain environment.

Shisir Khanal, Nepal’s foreign minister.  Photograph: Prakash Mathema/AFP/Getty Images

Its government has only been in power for six months, following protests that led to the collapse of the previous one. Nepal is estimated to be responsible for less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Andy Burnham: UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050 





On the day I became prime minister, I pledged to bring power to every postcode. Today, we begin to make good on that promise in the most literal sense. With nearly £30m of funding for People’s Power projects, communities across every nation of the UK will soon have the chance to build and control their own clean energy supply.
This investment means villages, towns and cities can harness the natural resources around them with solar panels on libraries, publicly owned windfarms, hydro schemes in their rivers, or whatever else works for them. The purpose is to put money back in people’s pockets while giving them a direct role in tackling the climate crisis.

Every council and community group awarded funding will have at least part-ownership in its renewable energy projects. That means, in the years ahead, more and more communities in Britain will do more than simply host solar panels and wind turbines. They will own a stake in them and retain a share of the wealth they create.


Today’s announcement is part of this government’s sustained effort to make energy more affordable. In my first week in office, I said I would remove VAT from household electricity bills. From the beginning of October, that policy kicks in, giving families some much-needed breathing room. But the only lasting way to bring down bills is to produce more of our own clean, renewable energy at home, which People’s Power will achieve.
I am acutely aware that our changing climate is a major concern for many Britons, not least because we have just emerged from our hottest summer on record. Punishing heatwaves left nurses collapsing on hospital wards and bus drivers working in 40C cabs. Wildfires destroyed homes, leaving families with nothing. And more extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead. The climate crisis is not a distant threat. It is here and with us now. The British people are no longer insulated from the consequences, and they do not want to be excluded from the solutions. They are looking for ways to do their bit. Community energy gives them that chance.
Across Britain, people are taking back control of the things that matter to them: their pubs, their libraries, their leisure centres. Some have already done the same with energy. Exclusive: PM, who is facing pressure over whether to approve North Sea oil and gasfields, makes strongest comments yet on issue 
 
 
British people understand the climate crisis threat. Today I’m empowering them to tackle it 
 
UK politics live – latest updates 




The UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050, Andy Burnham has argued in his strongest comments yet on the issue, saying it is no longer possible for Britons to believe they are not already affected by a changing climate.
Writing for the Guardian about new plans for a mass of community-led local green energy projects, the prime minister said the UK must “believe in itself”, and set out his determination to reach net zero targets, which have been rejected by the Conservatives and Reform UK.







British people understand the climate crisis threat. Today I’m empowering them to tackle it 
Andy Burnham


Read more
The tone marks a contrast to the summer, when Burnham faced criticism for a seemingly muted response to the heatwaves, droughts and wildfires that affected the UK, with his main initiative being a ban on portable barbecues.
“I am determined that we meet the commitment on which Labour was elected and reach net zero by 2050,” Burnham said. “I want Britain to believe in itself again.”
Saying he wanted to connect local communities to green power projects – to reach net zero targets and make energy more affordable – Burnham said: “I am acutely aware that our changing climate is a major concern for many Britons, not least because we have just emerged from our hottest summer on record.”


He went on: “Punishing heatwaves left nurses collapsing on hospital wards and bus drivers working in 40C cabs. Wildfires destroyed homes, leaving families with nothing. And more extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead.
“The climate crisis is not a distant threat. It is here and with us now. The British people are no longer insulated from the consequences, and they do not want to be excluded from the solutions. They are looking for ways to do their bit. Community energy gives them that chance.”
The issue is still a tricky one for Burnham, who is facing significant pressure from both sides over whether to approve the Jackdaw gasfield and Rosebank oilfield in the North Sea.
A number of Labour MPs believe approving the projects would send a negative signal on climate efforts, and would provide a boost to the Greens, who argue that Labour is insufficiently serious in tackling the climate emergency.
A seemingly imminent decision to approve Jackdaw has been delayed until later this autumn, prompting the Greens to accuse Labour of wanting to bury the issue before the high-profile Holborn and St Pancras byelection, where Zack Polanski, the leader of the Greens in England and Wales, is challenging for the seat vacated by Keir Starmer.


Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, had been poised to give her recommendation to approve the field off the coast of Aberdeen, but it has been put off.

 ‘I see them like my own children’: reforesting Ethiopia with 50bn trees, one step at a time


After losing much of its forests in recent decades, ordinary citizens have led the way in planting saplings across the country as part of the government’s Green Legacy Initiative




When Halima Kedir first began planting trees, she was met with scepticism and even mockery. “My neighbours discouraged me,” she recalls, sitting on a wooden chair in her garden, which is lush with the trees and fruits she has planted – banana, olive and grevillea among them.
“They thought I was striving for nothing, but with time, many are realising that trees can be part of the solution to our problems as a way to fight climate change and food insecurity,” she says.

Kedir, 35, who lives in the Berbere district of Ethiopia’s Oromia region, became an accidental environmentalist after planting thousands of trees – she has lost count of how many – inspiring others to follow suit.
In a nation with a history of large-scale deforestation, Kedir’s work has not been easy. It has required moral courage and practical endurance. As her trees took root and her surroundings became greener, the people who doubted began to respect what she was doing, she says. “Now, everything has changed. Those who tried to dissuade me are envious of my effort and commitment.”
For Kedir, trees are more than just plants, they are living companions and part of a solution to some of the challenges her community faces in one of the world’s most climate-vulnerable nations.
From the turn of the century to 2025, Ethiopia lost 560,000 hectares (2,160 sq miles) of its tree cover, due to the expansion of agriculture, commercial logging and the use of charcoal as fuel. This has resulted in devastating impacts on biodiversity, soil quality and water resources as well as increasing the risk of climate-related disasters.
But thanks to a number of initiatives introduced by the Ethiopian government, including a massive tree-planting scheme known as the Green Legacy Initiative (GLI) in 2019, the rate of deforestation has slowed. Between 2013 and 2023, the annual deforestation rate fell from 92,000 hectares to 27,703 hectares. Meanwhile, forest cover has increased from 15.5% to 23.6% during the same period.
Through the GLI, the government claims to have planted 48bn trees in seven years, including a reported record-breaking 353m seedlings in one day. Its goal is to plant 50bn trees by 2030.

The UK government is “cutting corners” on its commitments to provide climate aid, MPs have warned in a new report, just as a record-breaking ‘super’ El Niño weather event begins to intensify extreme weather and humanitarian crises around the world.
The International Development Committee said that cuts to the UK’s aid budget - which will result in the UK’s bilateral aid relationship essentially ending with a large group of countries - have undermined its ability to provide meaningful support to some of the world’s poorest and most climate-vulnerable countries.
Its report on “International Climate Finance” - a stream of foreign aid that rich countries are obligated to provide under the terms of the 2015 Paris Agreement - finds that successive reductions in the aid budget have damaged the UK’s ability to meet its climate commitments “in a meaningful, transparent and credible way”.




MPs also criticised changes to the way climate finance is accounted for, which allow existing humanitarian aid to be counted towards the UK’s climate spending commitments.
They said the government had prioritised maintaining headline spending figures “as opposed to striving to deliver genuine climate and nature outcomes”.

Sarah Champion, chair of the committee, said climate change was already “swiftly reversing development progress in vulnerable countries”, and warned that El Niño could worsen water insecurity and push more people into acute food shortages.


“Rather than striving to deliver genuine climate and nature outcomes, the government has been cutting corners to maintain headline climate spending commitments,” she said.
Catherine Pettengell, executive director of the Climate Action Network UK, which represents 45 civil society organisations working on climate, added: “Current ICF commitments fall far short of the UK’s fair share of the finance needed by low- and middle-income countries to tackle the climate crisis not of their making. 


“Today’s IDC report must serve as a wake-up call to this new government on the extent to which UK credibility and commitments have been eroded and undermined by cuts and creative accounting.”

articles.title: Nepal to use new flood study to claim millions from UN climate disaster fund
articles.raw_rss: A new study says climate change was a likely factor in the massive flood on the Nepal-Tibet border last month.

articles.jina_text:
Thousands of people are dead or missing after massive floods and landslides tore through the Nepal-Tibet border last month





Nepal plans to use a new study linking climate change to the deadly floods last month as the basis of a financial request from a United Nations fund.
The BBC understands that Nepal hopes to claim around $20m (£15m) from the UN Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, which helps countries affected by climate change.
Around 1,400 people have died in the disaster while 6,150 people remain missing in Nepal as of Wednesday, according official data.
The study by research group World Weather Attribution, published on Thursday, says climate change was a likely contributing factor in the avalanche of rock and ice that unleashed devastating floods on the Nepal-Tibet border last month.
There was "absolutely no doubt that human-induced climate change played a role here in the preconditioning of the disaster", said Dr Friederike Otto, an Imperial College London climatologist who co-authored the study.
Massive floods and landslides swept through border towns and villages in Nepal and Tibet, wiping out thousands of houses, destroying energy infrastructure and leaving thousands dead or missing.
Scientists say the floods were caused by a collapse of rock wall and glacier ice near the peak of Langtang Lirung, a mountain on Nepal's side of the Himalayas.
The study said the disaster was the result of a "compound event" caused by rising temperatures, thinning glaciers, thawing permafrost and pre-existing geological weaknesses














According to the study, July and August temperatures in the area were around 1.5C (2.7F) warmer "due to human influence on the climate".
Meanwhile, glaciers in the region had also been thinning by about half a metre (1.6ft) a year, which could weaken existing fractures and increase instability.
Heavy snowfall last October and November also added to a large amount of meltwater early this year.
Climate change, while not the only cause of the disaster, was a "destabilising factor acting on a pre-existing geological predisposition", the study said.
In the wake of the floods, Nepal's leaders have said the country needs around $5bn (£3.7bn) to rebuild itself.
The UN Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, which came into operation last year, requires countries to submit evidence proving that the losses they faced were caused by climate change.
Nepali officials had been preparing satellite and drone images, as well as preliminary reports, to back up its request to the fund.
But the World Weather Attribution report is now the strongest evidence for their claim that climate change was a significant factor in the collapse of rock and ice at Langtang Lirung, authorities say.





The report "will be the main basis of our claim as it has detailed what role climate has played in this disaster," said Maheshwar Dhakal, spokesperson for Nepal's Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment.

The US decision to remove limits on coal and gas plant emissions is rooted in a perception of manliness in these industries





You can impress a certain kind of person at a party by reciting the fact that there are more yoga instructors in the US than there are coalminers. In fact, the disparity is greater than this catchy phrasing suggests: there are actually more yoga instructors in the US than there are people employed in the entirely of the coalmining industry, miners and otherwise. It’s not even especially close: about 38,000 people in the US work in coal, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, compared to about 100,000 yoga instructors who are registered with the Yoga Alliance, an industry group.

articles.jina_text:
The UK has a major leakage problem. A fifth of water supplies are lost to leaking pipes, and hot weather has increased the colossal waste of this increasingly valuable resource. 
The combination of heatwaves and low rainfall we have seen in recent months has dried out the ground and contracted the soil. This means the 265,160-mile network of underground pipes will have lost support as the soil shifts, with the resulting movement causing cracks and leaks. 
Water companies in England and Wales are already leaking an astonishing 2.6 billion litres of treated water every day – enough to fill 1,150 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Parts of the UK, and the south and south east of England in particular, are running perilously low on water with most of the country currently in drought.

 
In England alone, 30 million people have had their water use restricted through measures such as hosepipe bans after the driest July on record saw just a tenth of the long-term average rainfall for the month, and less than half the long-term average in August. These have left already-strained reservoir levels nearly 20 per cent lower than usual at this time of the year, with recent rainfall doing little to replenish stocks. 
But all of this is nothing compared to what we can expect in the future. The Government is forecasting a five billion litre shortfall each day for households by 2050 as climate change and a growing population vastly increase the demand for water. 
The situation is so dire that it threatens Labour’s housebuilding targets, since water companies have a statutory requirement to supply water to all new homes and if they can’t supply enough they must inform the local authority who will block the development. 
So what can be done? Fixing leaks would be the obvious place to start. To be fair to them, water companies have succeeded in cutting leaks by 40 per cent since their peak in the mid-1990s. But with such a vast network of pipes, many of them laid in the Victorian era, they have only pledged to fix half the remaining leaks by 2050 – and even that looks like a pretty tall order.



 
New reservoirs are the other big hope, with 10 new ones planned to open by 2050. They would be the first in the UK since the early 1990s.

Seven of the 10 most economically deprived constituencies had low access to nature.


After a spring and summer of extreme heat across England, when some cities and towns saw temperatures of 38C, the Wildlife Trusts said there was increased need for cool, shady and nature-rich spaces. It is seeking a meeting with ministers to present its green paper.

Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic floods and killing over a thousand people in Nepal and Tibet last month, the first scientific study of the disaster has found.
Researchers identified unusually warm conditions before the glacier’s collapse, which sent an avalanche of 110m cubic metres (3,885bn cu ft) of snow and ice into the valley below. This triggered flash floods on an almost unprecedented scale, hitting communities downstream without warning.








How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guide

Read more
“Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away,” said Dr Friederike Otto, a climate science professor at Imperial College London, which carried out the study.
“When warming destabilises the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction. Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come.”


View image in fullscreen
A impromptu memorial in Kathmandu commemorates some of the people killed in the flooding. Photograph: Narendra Shrestha/EPA
More than 1,300 people were killed and more than 5,000 people remain missing after a massive section of overhanging glacier and rock measuring roughly 200,000 sq metres (2,153,000 sq ft) fell from Langtang Lirung mountain on 26 August.
It dropped about 1,400 metres (4,660ft), slamming into the valley floor with such intensity that it registered as an earthquake, liquidising ice and sparking a freezing flood that careened downriver at speeds exceeding 110 mph.
The devastating flood of water, ice, rock and sediment swept away families, homes, settlements, roads, bridges and other infrastructure, leaving survivors stranded and cut off.
“Rock avalanches of this size are rare, with annual frequency estimates of approximately one event this size every 1,000–10,000 years,” the study said. “This event shows that limits to adaptation are already being reached.”
The research was unlike previous studies by Otto and her team at World Weather Attribution (WWA) – a collaborative project between Imperial and other climate specialists worldwide – in that the role of climate breakdown could not be ascribed to one particular weather event.
Instead, the researchers found the disaster was the result of a compound crisis, with a number of factors made worse by decades of atmospheric heating as a result of greenhouse gas pollution.

Company behind failed Surrey oilfield project sells site at massive loss


New owners apply for permission to extract oil in Horse Hill despite landmark ruling from supreme court in 2024




After years of trying to dig for oil in Surrey, the company behind the drilling project that was turned down in a landmark supreme court ruling has sold off the site for a fraction of the money it spent on it, and rebranded as a clean energy company.
Meanwhile, the new owners, who picked up the site for £1m, are applying, once again, for permission to dig.

UK Oil and Gas (UKOG) spent more than a decade trying to develop Horse Hill oilfields, where they said they had found 100bn barrels of oil. But in 2024 the supreme court, in a decision which has since become known as the Finch Ruling, decreed that “a planning authority should have considered the indirect downstream greenhouse gas emissions of an oil and gas project as part of its environmental impact assessment” and overturned a council decision to let expansion go ahead.


The Guardian understands that the implied value of the Horse Hill licence area reached a peak of £46m in September 2018 after UKOG agreed to buy a 14.3% economic stake from a group of vendors for £6.6m. The surging valuations given to the fields was driven by industry estimates that there could be about 9.24bn barrels of oil in the tight Jurassic shale and conventional reservoir sections within the Horse Hill licences.
Public records appear to show UKOG invested more than £25m into the site. Prior to the £1m sale, UKOG’s financial accounts showed that it had written down the value of its Horse Hill interests to just £55,360 on its balance sheet.
UKOG has now changed its name to UK Energy Group, seeking to shift its focus towards salt-cavern energy storage and other clean energy projects.
Stephen Sanderson, the company’s chief executive, said while the company still sees “potentially material resources” at Horse Hill, the divestment presented “timely and attractive opportunity to complete UKOG’s exit from the UK onshore oil and gas sector”.
The company reportedly raised £1m in 2025 to develop hydrogen-storage projects in south Dorset and Yorkshire, and a further £500,000 to acquire land for a proposed East Yorkshire salt-cavern site.

Climate Change Committee says government cannot expand airport without requiring aviation industry to clean up its emissions 




Heathrow airport should be allowed to expand only if airlines pay for the removal of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, the government’s climate advisers have said.
Building a third runway and new terminals, as some in government want to do, would breach the UK’s carbon budgets and make reaching net zero by 2050 impossible, on current policies, according to the Climate Change Committee.

The “only way” to manage such expansion within the UK’s climate commitments was for the aviation industry to become more efficient, use an increasing proportion of “sustainable aviation fuels” (SAF) in place of fossil fuels, and pay for the permanent removal and storage of carbon from the atmosphere.


Nigel Topping, the chair of the CCC, said: “The government cannot expand Heathrow airport without requiring the aviation industry to clean up its emissions. Therefore, the government should legislate policies that require the aviation industry to fully address all of their emissions by 2050, either directly or by purchasing engineered removals. The polluter-pays principle must apply.”
In a report to the government on Wednesday, the CCC found that the costs of SAF and carbon removal would probably be passed on to passengers by airlines, adding an estimated £150 to the price of a return flight to Alicante by 2050, or about £400 to the price of a flight to New York. These costs would be phased in gradually over 25 years.
But campaigners rejected the CCC’s plan of relying on nascent technologies to wipe out the impact of an expansion that would commit the UK to much higher emissions for decades, and called on ministers to halt all airport expansion.
Tony Bosworth, campaigner at Friends of the Earth, accused the CCC of “pulling its punches”, pointing to recent research by the Tyndall Centre that found SAF and carbon removals were unproven and unlikely to ramp up in time to the extent needed to justify airport expansion.


“The CCC should have made it crystal clear: there is no plausible way to expand Heathrow without wrecking the UK’s climate targets,” he said.
Frequent flying is overwhelming skewed towards the wealthy. Exposure to air pollution from traffic and fossil fuels could increase the risk of death by suicide, according to a new study that pooled data from dozens of studies conducted around the world.
Researchers at Queen's University Belfast combined data from 29 studies to examine whether pollutants, including fine particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide, were linked to suicide risk. 
The study found that both short-term and long-term exposure to PM2.5, tiny airborne particles mainly produced by traffic and the burning of fossil fuels, were linked to significantly greater odds of death by suicide, attempted suicide and suicidal thoughts. 




Short-term exposure to PM10, a larger particulate pollutant, and long-term exposure to nitrogen dioxide were also linked to increased risk, while a broader review of existing literature suggested possible links to other pollutants, including sulphur dioxide and ozone, and to noise pollution. The findings are published in the Journal of Epidemiology & Community Health.
More than 720,000 people die by suicide worldwide each year but the true figure is thought to be higher due to underreporting. The WHO has set a goal of cutting the global suicide rate by a third between 2013 and 2030. 

“These findings bring to attention the critical importance of recognising environmental exposures as modifiable risk factors within suicide prevention efforts," the study noted. “Integrating environmental health into mental health policy, through cross-sectoral collaboration, pollution reduction strategies, and targeted public health interventions, could play a vital role in reducing suicide risk and improving overall population mental wellbeing."



A woman carries a sack of garbage beside burning plastic wastage (Getty)
The researchers noted that air pollutants had previously been associated with chronic inflammation and damage to the nervous system, which could impair brain function and affect mood, while traffic and other environmental noise could raise stress levels by disrupting the body's natural sleep-wake cycle. 


Water pollution and noise pollution showed potential links in the wider literature review, though the evidence for water and light pollution was too limited or inconsistent to draw firm conclusions.


Experts who weren’t associated with the study said the findings were an important contribution, but urged caution in how they were interpreted. 
Alexander Larcombe, associate professor at Curtin University's School of Population Health, said the results more likely reflected the fact that polluted areas tended to be more disadvantaged, with higher unemployment, social isolation, and poorer access to mental health care, all of which independently raise suicide risk.

Bristol has become the first British city to impose a ban on the advertising of fast fashion, in new restrictions that will also curb ads for SUVs and airlines.
The ban is part of moves by the West Country city, known for its radical political scene, to impose sweeping bans on advertising for polluting industries.

Restrictions have also been placed on advertising SUVs, airlines, cruises and fossil fuels on advertising sites owned by the Green-run council.
“We don’t want Bristol to be a billboard for polluters while we’re working hard to improve health, air quality and nature in the city,” said Heather Mack, Bristol city council’s deputy leader.
“We’re proud to be thinking holistically about the changes we need to keep Bristol green and thriving.”


Bristol council’s strategy and resources committee passed the new advertising and sponsorship policy by an eight to one vote on Monday. It updates a policy passed in 2021 which made Bristol the first council outside London to ban junk food ads.

The policy will apply to all council-owned advertising space, including billboards, bus stop shelters, print and online.

The change in policy reflects political trends in the city, which elected the Green party’s Carla Denyer as MP in 2024, the same year that voters made the Green party the largest party in the council chamber. “It makes no sense for these efforts to be running alongside advertisements for things like oil and gas companies, SUVs or fast fashion which do not align with our community values.”

Firms manage $7.3tn in assets and could afford to transition away from fossil fuels yet invest in natural gas and coal-fired plants to power datacenters




The energy portfolios of 20 private equity firms produce 1.5bn tons of greenhouse gases a year, more than the annual emissions of any country except China, the US, India and Russia, according to a new report.
Together, these firms manage $7.3tn in assets of all kinds, affording them the ability to shape the pace of the transition away from fossil fuels. However their energy investments include significant fossil fuel assets including natural gas and coal-fired power plants to provide electricity to datacenters.

The analysis of the top 20 private equity firms invested in global energy infrastructure was conducted by the Private Equity Climate Risks Consortium. It found that the firms owned 15,000 miles of pipelines, 124GW of power generation capacity across 370 fossil fuel-powered plants and hundreds of oil and gas fields.


Half of the top 10 US datacenter owners are backed by private equity, said Matt Parr, the communications director for Private Equity Stakeholder Project (PESP), one of the organizations in the Private Equity Climate Risks Consortium. “This industry doesn’t get enough scrutiny and credit for its contribution to global emissions,” Parr said. “It’s a very opaque business model.”
The research team queried energy holdings with the private markets data provider PitchBook, drawing on additional details from company websites, press releases, news articles and regulatory filings. Because of gaps in the data, the researchers were unable to calculate how much the 20 private equity firms invested in fossil fuel assets. But an earlier analysis of data compiled on PitchBook shows that private equity has funded more than $1tn in fossil fuel assets since 2010, said Amanda Mendoza, senior research and campaign coordinator on the climate team at the Private Equity Stakeholder Project.
While some public-sector retirement systems have been trying to limit their exposure to fossil fuel projects, the private equity firms BlackRock, GIP, Energy Capital Partners, EQT and Kayne Anderson increased the amount of fossil fuel companies in their portfolio compared with 2024, according to the report.


The private equity firm EQT has positioned itself as a climate conscious investor, supporting the energy transition. But EQT, along with Blackrock’s GIP and the California Public Employees’ Retirement system could soon acquire AES Corporation, which owns more than 20 power plants. “It is alarming because if this deal does go through they will then be owners of a fleet of coal power and gas powered plants,” Mendoza said. “That’s significantly going to impact their transition. It seems like they’re transitioning to fossil fuels instead of away.”
